The weakest point is the thing you're proudest of, and it's not the phone-only principle itself — it's that phone-only collides head-on with "I work alone, 8 to 6, hands in a bike all day."

Think through what actually happens. A customer rings at 11am. You're elbow-deep in a bottom bracket at someone's house. You either:

- stop, wipe your hands, answer, and lose five minutes plus your flow on every call (and the customer in front of you watches you take other people's calls), or
- let it ring to voicemail — in which case your "talk to a real person" promise has just delivered the customer to a machine, which is the exact thing you built the policy to avoid.

Then you ring back at 6:30pm, they don't pick up, and you're playing phone tag for a £40 job. Multiply that by 300 regulars plus walk-ins, and a meaningful chunk of your bookings will leak away — not because people dislike phoning, but because nobody can reach you. The people most likely to give up are the new customers you don't have a relationship with yet, which is exactly where growth comes from.

The rest of the plan is genuinely solid: qualified, equipped, insured, inherited customer base, low overhead. The one structural gap is that you have a one-person business with a booking channel that requires a person to be free during working hours, and that person isn't free.

Ways to keep the heart of the idea without the hole:

- **Keep phone as the primary channel, but add a safety net** — a simple text or online form saying "request a callback," so a missed call isn't a lost customer. You still call everyone back personally; you've just caught them first.
- **A proper voicemail that sets a promise** — "I'm mid-repair, I'll ring you back before 7 tonight" — and then actually do it, every day, as a fixed 30-minute block.
- **Part-time phone cover** — a partner, a retired mate, a call-answering service for a few quid a day. "Every customer talks to a real person" doesn't have to mean *you*.
- **Track missed calls for the first month.** If you're missing 20+ a week, you'll have your answer in data rather than my opinion.

You can absolutely keep the human-contact principle. Just don't let the booking channel depend on the one person who's never available to pick up.

Think about what a booking call actually looks like from your side: you're mid-job, hands greasy, maybe halfway through bleeding a brake. The phone rings. You either stop (cost: time, a half-finished job, grease on the phone, a customer in front of you watching you take another customer's call) or you let it go to voicemail. Most people won't leave a voicemail, and many won't call back — they'll ring the next mechanic on the list, or go back to a shop with a website. Your 300 inherited regulars will tolerate this for a while because they know you. New customers won't. So your main acquisition channel is also your biggest leak.

The good news is you don't have to abandon the principle. "Every customer talks to a real person" is a fine idea; "every customer talks to *me, live, whenever they call*" is the version that doesn't work. Options:

- **Set a call-back promise instead of a live-answer promise.** Voicemail greeting says "I'm under a bike, leave your name and number and I'll call back by 1pm / 6pm." Then actually do it, every day, at fixed times. People accept this from tradespeople.
- **Allow text/WhatsApp for first contact**, then you call them back. It's still a person-to-person conversation, just not at the moment they happen to ring.
- **Pay for a part-time answering service or a local person** (a few hours a day) to take calls and book slots in a shared calendar. Cheap relative to lost jobs.
- **Block an hour a day for the phone** and tell customers that's when you're reachable live.

One more thing, smaller: being phone-only also means being findable-only-by-word-of-mouth. You don't need an app, but a one-page Google Business listing with your number and hours costs nothing and is how people will find your phone number in the first place.

The weakest point is the phone-only booking combined with working alone.

You'll be under a bike or in a customer's driveway from 8 to 6, so you'll miss most calls. A missed call from someone who has never used you usually becomes a booking for a competitor, because people rarely leave voicemails or call back. Your 300 regulars will probably put up with it, but new customers, who you need for growth, are the ones most likely to drop out.

Some facts that bear on it:
- Many people, especially under 40, prefer to book online or by text, and some will not phone at all.
- Calls taken while working are interrupted, and you'll be fielding them with greasy hands, in noise, without your diary in front of you.
- Without a website, you are largely invisible in local searches ("bike repair near me") and on Google Maps, which is a main source of new mobile-service customers.

You can keep the idea of talking to a real person without losing bookings:
- Set aside fixed call-back windows (e.g. 8-8:30 and 6-7pm) and say so in your voicemail message.
- Offer text or WhatsApp as a way to request a call, and still have the conversation by phone.
- Set up a free Google Business Profile with your number and hours, and a simple one-page site with a "request a call back" form. This is not an online booking system, and it still ends in a conversation.

Secondary risks: no cover when you're ill or on holiday, and travel time between jobs reducing the number of billable hours per day.

P3'.answer:
The weakest point is phone-only booking combined with working alone, out on jobs, with your hands in a bike from 8 to 6. Those two choices work against each other.

- **You can't answer the phone during the hours people call.** Most people ring during the working day, usually on a break, and if you don't pick up, many won't leave a voicemail. They'll search for the next repairer who responds. Every missed call is a lost job, and as a new business you can't afford that.
- **Answering mid-job costs you too.** Stopping to take calls breaks your concentration, slows the repair, and can sound rushed or distracted on the customer's end, which undercuts the "real person" experience you want.
- **Some customers will never phone.** Many people, especially under 40, will text or book online rather than call. You'd be turning away part of your market for the sake of a principle.

Your 300 regulars will probably ring you, so the problem won't show up straight away. It will show up when you try to grow beyond them.

You can keep the heart of the idea, which is that a real person is involved, without making the phone the only door:

1. **Set callback windows.** Have a voicemail say, "I'm out on a job, I return calls at 12:30 and 5:30." People accept this from a tradesperson.
2. **Accept texts or WhatsApp** as well as calls, so people can reach you in a few seconds and you can reply between jobs.
3. **Add a one-page website** with your number, your area, your prices, and a "request a callback" form. It can say you'll phone everyone personally to confirm. That keeps the human contact and fixes discoverability.

A few smaller risks are worth checking. Travel time between jobs cuts into billable hours, so your pricing should account for it. And as a solo operator, illness or a van breakdown stops all income. Neither is as serious as the phone issue.

You've done the hard parts well: the skills, the van, the insurance, and a ready customer base. The booking method is the one decision that could undermine them, and it's cheap to fix.
